acs64.about: Amtrak Cities Sprinter, an electric locomotive that pulls Northeast Regional and Keystone Service trains on the electrified Northeast Corridor and Harrisburg line. It replaced Amtrak's aging AEM-7 and HHP-8 fleets, and its first revenue run was a Boston to Washington Northeast Regional on February 7, 2014.

amfleet.about: The short-distance coach that makes up most Northeast Regional and Keystone trains, based on the Budd Metroliner design. Many were refurbished with fewer seats (from 84 to 72), and Amtrak plans to begin retiring the Amfleet I fleet in 2027 as Airo trainsets arrive.

amfleet2.about: A long-distance version of the Amfleet with larger windows, more legroom and a single vestibule, used on trains such as the Palmetto and other Eastern long-distance routes. They were the last passenger cars Budd built.

amfleetBusiness.about: An Amfleet I car fitted with wider, roomier seating for business class on Northeast Corridor trains. Several were created by rebuilding the older club cars.

amfleetCafe.about: An Amfleet I car with a snack bar and some coach seating, used on Northeast Corridor and Keystone trains. Some café cars were later reconfigured into club-dinettes and all-table dinettes.

metrolinerCab.about: A former Metroliner electric multiple-unit car whose traction gear was removed and a control cab added, so a locomotive can push a train from the far end. Used mainly on Keystone Service and the Hartford Line and Valley Flyer in New England, and expected to be replaced by Airo trainsets.

acelaPower.about: Each NextGen Acela trainset has a power car at each end, together producing about 9,400 hp. The trains entered service on August 28, 2025, and are limited to 160 mph by Northeast Corridor track and signals, though the design allows higher speeds.

acelaCoach.about: A trailer car in the articulated NextGen Acela trainset, which seats 386 in total across First Class and Business Class. It replaces the original Acela Express trains on the Northeast Corridor, with tilting to hold speed through curves.

genesis.about: Amtrak's standard diesel locomotive since the 1990s, built as 207 units numbered 1 to 207. Siemens Chargers are replacing them on long-distance trains, and some units are being converted into P42C non-powered control units.

p32.about: A diesel locomotive that can also draw power from the third rail, so it can run into New York Penn Station. Amtrak uses its 18 units only north of New York City on the Empire Service, Ethan Allen Express, Adirondack, Maple Leaf and the Lake Shore Limited's New York section, and plans to replace them with Airo trainsets.

alc42.about: Amtrak's long-distance version of the Charger, with a longer nose and a bigger fuel tank than the state-corridor SC-44. The first entered service on the Empire Builder on February 8, 2022, and it is replacing the Genesis fleet.

alc42@amtrak/Amtrak Cascades.about: A Charger variant bought as part of Amtrak's Airo procurement. Three of the eight Airo trainsets on Amtrak Cascades use it, with the other five using existing SC-44s, and the first entered Cascades service on September 30, 2026.

charger@amtrak.about: The state-owned version of the Charger, bought by Illinois and the Midwest states (33), Caltrans in California (24) and Washington (Cascades).

venture@amtrak.fleet: About 97 Venture cars in the Midwest
venture@amtrak.about: A single-level coach built in Florin, California, for Amtrak's Midwest corridors including the Hiawatha, Lincoln Service and Wolverine. Many run as semi-permanently coupled married pairs.

venture@amtrak/San Joaquins.fleet: 49 cars (seven sets) on the San Joaquins
venture@amtrak/San Joaquins.about: A single-level coach used on California's San Joaquins, which is now branded Gold Runner. Trains run as seven-car sets that include a cab car.

venture@amtrak/Amtrak Cascades.about: A Siemens Venture-based coach in the Airo trainsets for the Pacific Northwest corridor. Each Cascades set is six cars: business, café, three coaches and a coach-baggage-cab car, and service began September 30, 2026.

ventureCab@amtrak.about: A Venture coach with an engineer's cab so a train can be run push-pull. The Midwest cab cars are for the Hiawatha service between Chicago and Milwaukee.

ventureCab@amtrak/San Joaquins.fleet: 7 (one per set) on the San Joaquins
ventureCab@amtrak/San Joaquins.about: A Venture coach with an engineer's cab, running at one end of each seven-car San Joaquins set so the train can be driven from either end. The route is now branded Gold Runner.

ventureCab@amtrak/Amtrak Cascades.about: The coach-baggage-cab car at one end of each six-car Airo set on Amtrak Cascades. It lets the train be driven from either end, so the locomotive does not need to be turned.

californiaCar.about: A bi-level car owned by Caltrans and Amtrak, used on the Capitol Corridor and Gold Runner (San Joaquins) in California. The fleet includes coaches, coach-baggage cars, cab cars and café cars, and Caltrans overhauled the cars about ten years early after door problems.

californiaCab.about: The cab and coach version of the California Car, used as the control car for push-pull trains on the Capitol Corridor and Gold Runner. All 14 were named after California mountains.

surfliner.fleet: About 37 non-cab cars on Amtrak's roster
surfliner.about: A bi-level car for Southern California, built at Hornell, New York, as a refinement of the Superliner and California Car designs. Amtrak and Caltrans own the type, and it runs on the Pacific Surfliner and other California corridors.

surflinerCab.about: The cab, baggage and coach version of the Surfliner bi-level car, used as the control car for push-pull trains. The checked baggage space is on the lower level, which leaves the upper level for passenger seating.

f59.about: A 3,200 hp diesel built for commuter and state-supported corridor service. Caltrans owns 15 for California routes, and North Carolina owns two for the Piedmont, where it also runs older F59PH units.

coach@amtrak/Piedmont.builder: Pullman-Standard / St. Louis Car Company (rebuilt for NCDOT)
coach@amtrak/Piedmont.about: A 1960s-built coach originally made for Kansas City Southern and Union Pacific, refurbished by North Carolina's DOT with new seats, wiring and plumbing. They are state-owned and named after North Carolina landmarks, running on the Piedmont between Raleigh and Charlotte. NCDOT has won federal grants to replace them with new cars.

viewlinerSleeper.about: The single-level sleeper used on Amtrak's Eastern long-distance trains such as the Lake Shore Limited and Silver Meteor. The Viewliner I has 12 roomettes with in-room toilets, and the later Viewliner II has 11 roomettes and shared restrooms, and runs to 125 mph.

viewlinerDiner.about: A full-service dining car built in Elmira, New York, for Eastern long-distance trains. It replaced the old Heritage Fleet diners.

viewlinerBaggage.about: A baggage car for Eastern long-distance trains, built in Elmira, New York, with the first entering service on March 23, 2015. It replaced all of the old Heritage Fleet baggage cars.

superlinerCoach.about: The bi-level coach used on Amtrak's western long-distance trains such as the Empire Builder and California Zephyr. Superliners are too tall for the Northeast Corridor tunnels, and Amtrak plans to replace them by about 2032.

superlinerSleeper.about: A bi-level sleeper with roomettes and bedrooms, including family and accessible bedrooms, used on western long-distance trains. Superliner II added a few deluxe sleepers with their own bathrooms.

superlinerDiner.about: A bi-level dining car with the dining room on the upper level and the kitchen below, used on western long-distance trains. Superliners run on 480 V head-end power and cannot operate on the Northeast Corridor because of tunnel clearances.

superlinerLounge.about: A lounge car with large wraparound windows on the upper level for scenic views, with a café below. It is used on western long-distance trains.

autorack.about: A bi-level enclosed car that carries passengers' vehicles on the Auto Train between Lorton, Virginia, and Sanford, Florida. Amtrak replaced its older autoracks with about 80 new ones, and a train can carry up to about 340 vehicles.

charger@via.about: VIA Rail's Charger is the locomotive at the head of each Venture trainset in the Québec City–Windsor corridor, where it replaced the aging F40PH and LRC-era equipment. It is designed for 125 mph, but VIA limits passenger service to about 100 mph. Each of VIA's 32 Charger-and-Venture trainsets is a fixed set with one locomotive.

venture@via.fleet: 128 coaches with VIA Rail (64 business, 64 economy)
venture@via.about: The Venture is the coach in VIA Rail's fixed five-car corridor trainsets, built at Siemens' Sacramento plant. Each set has two business-class and two economy coaches plus an economy cab car, and is pushed or pulled by a Charger locomotive. Economy coaches seat about 66 and business coaches about 44.

ventureCab@via.about: The economy-class cab car at one end of each of VIA Rail's 32 five-car Venture trainsets in the Québec City–Windsor corridor. It holds the engineer's cab so the set can run push-pull with the Charger locomotive at the other end. Built by Siemens in Sacramento, California.

f40@via.about: The F40PH-2 has been VIA Rail's main passenger locomotive since the late 1980s, hauling the Canadian, the Ocean and regional trains. VIA rebuilt the fleet starting in 2007, adding separate head-end power generators (the rebuilt units are often called F40PH-2D), and a further rebuild to extend life toward 2035 has been reported. Siemens Chargers are replacing them on corridor trains.

buddBaggage.about: A stainless-steel baggage car that VIA took over from Canadian Pacific in 1978 and still uses on the Canadian and other long-distance trains. It can carry about a dozen canoes and more than 100 large suitcases, and is heated for pets. Most were built for CP in 1954–55; some came later, in 1963.

buddCoach.about: Stainless-steel coaches built by Budd for Canadian railways and rebuilt for head-end power, now used on the Canadian and the Ocean. VIA's 8100-series cars seat about 62 and its 4100-series cars about 68. They are among the oldest passenger cars in regular intercity service in North America.

buddDiner.about: A stainless-steel dining car built for Canadian Pacific's 1955 Canadian and rebuilt by AMF; it has a full kitchen and seats 48 (a few cars seat 44). VIA runs these on the Canadian between Toronto and Vancouver.

buddSleeper.about: The Manor is a Budd stainless-steel sleeper built for Canadian Pacific's Canadian and Dominion; VIA acquired all 42 in 1978. After VIA's rebuild, a car has sections, roomettes and double bedrooms, plus a shower added in place of one section. About 40 remain on the Canadian and other VIA long-distance trains.

skyline.about: A stainless-steel dome car built for Canadian Pacific in 1954–55 and taken over by VIA in 1978. VIA rebuilt it with a dining room and snack bar below and a dome above, seating 24 in the dining room and 24 in the dome. It runs mid-train on the Canadian; the name came from the Skyline Trail Hikers.

parkCar.about: A Budd stainless-steel car that combines sleeping rooms (three double bedrooms and one triple), a 24-seat dome, a bar and a rounded observation lounge at the rear. Built for Canadian Pacific and named for parks, they run at the back of the Canadian and also appear on the Jasper–Prince Rupert train and the Ocean.

renaissanceCoach.about: Built in Britain for the Nightstar overnight service through the Channel Tunnel, which was cancelled; VIA bought the unused cars in December 2000 and rebuilt them in Thunder Bay for service from 2002. VIA uses them on the Ocean between Montreal and Halifax. The design derives from British Rail's Mark 4 coach.

renaissanceSleeper.about: Built for the Nightstar service through the Channel Tunnel and bought by VIA in 2000 after that service was cancelled. Each car has 10 double-occupancy rooms, all with a toilet and about half with a shower. VIA uses them on the Ocean between Montreal and Halifax.

renaissanceDiner.about: A dining car in the Renaissance fleet that VIA bought from the cancelled Nightstar service; it seats 48 (32 at tables for four, 16 at tables for two) and has a take-out counter and some baggage space. VIA also has about 20 Renaissance service cars (lounge and staff bedroom). They run on the Ocean between Montreal and Halifax.

rdc@via.fleet: About 5 in service with VIA Rail
rdc@via.about: The RDC was a self-propelled diesel railcar sold to railroads across North America from 1949. VIA's cars, built 1955–58, run the Sudbury–White River service in northern Ontario (long known as the Lake Superior train), one of the last regular Budd RDC runs. Some of VIA's cars are RDC-4 baggage-and-mail units with no passenger seats.

charger@brightline.about: Brightline runs a Charger at each end of its Venture trainsets in Florida, 10 delivered for the original Miami–West Palm Beach service and 11 more in 2023 for the Orlando extension. The Orlando extension has track speeds up to 125 mph. The SCB-40 has a streamlined nose and 4,000 hp, a bit less than the 4,400 hp SC-44.

venture@brightline.about: Brightline's Venture coaches run in trainsets between two Charger locomotives, with no cab cars. Smart (standard) coaches seat 66 in a 2×2 layout and Premium coaches seat 50 in 2×1. Sets have been lengthened from four cars to as many as ten.

m7.about: The M7 is the backbone of the Long Island Rail Road's electric fleet, running as married pairs on third-rail lines. It is designed for 100 mph but limited to 80 mph in service. Power is about 1,060 hp per car; the A car seats about 110 and the B car about 101.

m9.about: The M9 entered LIRR service in September 2019, years behind schedule, and is the newest electric car on the railroad. It is designed for 100 mph but limited to 80 mph in service. An Alstom-built M9A order, for 160 LIRR cars, will replace the M3s; power is about 1,100 hp per car.

m3.about: The M3 is the Long Island Rail Road's oldest electric car, built at Budd's Red Lion plant in Philadelphia. It is slated to be retired and replaced by new M9A cars, but remains in service because M9 deliveries were delayed. It is designed for 100 mph but limited to 80 mph in service.

c3.about: A double-deck, push-pull coach used on LIRR diesel and dual-mode trains east of Jamaica, pulled by DE30AC and DM30AC locomotives. Seating is 2–2, unlike the 3–2 layout on the earlier C1 cars. Trailers with a toilet seat about 137 and plain trailers about 143.

c3Cab.about: The control car at the end of an LIRR bi-level push-pull train, with an engineer's cab so the locomotive can push from the rear. It also has a restroom and seats about 137. The LIRR has 134 C3 cars in all, built by Kawasaki.

de30ac.about: A diesel-only locomotive that, with the dual-mode DM30AC, pulls the LIRR's C3 bi-level trains. It was built at the Super Steel plant in Schenectady, New York. One unit, 423, was converted from a DM30AC. Siemens Chargers are on order to replace the DE30ACs and DM30ACs.

dm30ac.about: A dual-mode locomotive that runs on diesel or on third-rail electric power, so LIRR trains can run into Penn Station and Grand Central Madison without a change of engine. It makes 3,000 hp on diesel and about 2,880 hp on third rail, and tops out at 80 mph on electric power. Siemens Chargers are on order to replace it.

m7a.about: The Metro-North version of the LIRR's M7, running on the electrified Hudson and Harlem lines out of Grand Central. It is designed for 100 mph but limited to 80 mph in service. Power is about 1,060 hp per car; the A car seats about 110 and the B car about 101.

m8.about: The M8 runs on Metro-North's New Haven Line and branches, and is shared with Connecticut's Shore Line East. It entered service in March 2011, replacing the M2, M4 and M6 fleets, and is limited to 80 mph on Metro-North. Power is about 1,080 hp per car; A cars seat 111 and B cars 101.

shoreliner@mnr.about: A push-pull coach used on Metro-North's diesel territory, mainly the non-electrified Hudson, Harlem and New Haven line branches, behind P32AC-DM and Charger locomotives. About 184 Shoreliner cars (coaches and cab cars, in four series) are in the fleet, some owned by Connecticut DOT. Metro-North issued a request for about 252 replacement coaches in 2026, with deliveries expected to start around 2029.

shorelinerCab@mnr.about: A Shoreliner coach fitted with an engineer's cab, so Metro-North's diesel push-pull trains can be driven from the rear with the locomotive pushing. About 184 Shoreliner cars (coaches and cab cars) run on Metro-North, some owned by Connecticut DOT. They are slated for replacement under a procurement started in 2026.

p32@mnr.about: A GE Genesis-family dual-mode locomotive that runs on diesel or Metro-North's third rail, letting diesel-hauled trains run into Grand Central. In electric mode it is limited to 60 mph. Some units are owned by Connecticut DOT; Siemens Chargers are replacing them, and No. 221 was sold to the Adirondack Railroad in 2026.

genesis@mnr.about: Metro-North's Genesis is the GE P32AC-DM, a dual-mode locomotive that runs on diesel or third rail so diesel-hauled trains can run into Grand Central. In electric mode it is limited to 60 mph. Siemens Chargers are replacing them.

charger@mnr.about: A diesel and third-rail dual-mode locomotive, replacing Metro-North's P32AC-DM fleet. The first two arrived in October 2024 and revenue service began on September 22, 2025, between Grand Central and Poughkeepsie. It makes 4,200 hp on diesel and about 2,100 hp on third rail; Metro-North expects a 110 mph service speed.

alp46.about: NJ Transit's electric locomotive for the Northeast Corridor and North Jersey Coast and Morristown lines, based on the German DB Class 101. They replaced the ALP-44s and other older electrics. The ALP-46A is rated for 125 mph and about 7,500 hp, but NJ Transit limits both types to 100 mph.

multilevel.fleet: About 430 MultiLevel I/II cars; MultiLevel III on order
multilevel.about: NJ Transit's bi-level push-pull coach, in use since 2006 on both electric and diesel lines. Trailers seat about 142 (about 133 with a restroom). In 2025 NJ Transit ordered 200 more MultiLevel III cars, which include powered cars and will be built by Alstom through 2031.

multilevelCab.fleet: 62 MultiLevel I/II cab cars; MultiLevel III on order
multilevelCab.about: The control car at one end of an NJ Transit bi-level push-pull train, with an engineer's cab so the locomotive can push from the rear. Cab cars seat about 127–130. NJ Transit has 52 MultiLevel I and 10 MultiLevel II cab cars, with MultiLevel III cab cars on order from Alstom.

hsp46.about: The HSP46 is the MBTA's newest commuter rail locomotive, numbered 2000–2039 and in service since April 2014. It replaced diesels dating to the late 1970s and uses a GE GEVO-12 engine. MBTA trains are limited to 79 mph, and Wabtec is due to overhaul all 40 units by 2032.

f40c.about: The F40PH-3C is a rebuilt F40PH. The MBTA's units were built in 1987–88 by EMD and in 1991–93 by Morrison-Knudsen, then rebuilt by MotivePower in 2001–04 and again as F40PH-3Cs starting in 2019. They are numbered 1025–1036 and 1050–1075.

gp40.builder: GM Diesel (built as GP40-2LW for Canadian National); rebuilt by AMF
gp40.about: The GP40MC is an EMD GP40-2LW originally built for Canadian National and rebuilt for MBTA passenger service in the late 1990s. They are numbered 1115–1139 and 1776. The 3,000 hp rating is the standard GP40 figure.

mp36@mbta.about: The MBTA bought these two locomotives, numbered 010 and 011, from Utah's FrontRunner in 2011. They are the only MP36s on the MBTA roster and were out of service for overhaul as of early 2026.

bilevel@mbta.about: These bi-level coaches have been the backbone of MBTA Commuter Rail since 1990, built by Kawasaki (1990–2006) and by Hyundai Rotem (2012–2014 and 2022–2024). More Rotem coaches are on order for 2026–27. Seat counts range from 178 to 185 depending on the series.

rotemCab.about: The CTC-5 lets a train be driven from the rear end in push-pull service. The MBTA has 71 in service, numbered 1800–1870, with 10 more on order. They were the first new bi-level cab cars since the Kawasaki CTC-4.

kawasakiCab.about: The CTC-4 is a cab car from the MBTA's first Kawasaki bi-level order and is numbered 1700–1724. Alstom overhauled the fleet in 2014–2019, and the cars now look nearly identical to the Hyundai Rotem cars.

single@mbta.about: These older single-level coaches are the MBTA's oldest passenger cars: Pullman (1978–79), MBB (1987–88) and Bombardier (1987–90). Most Bombardier BTC-1A and BTC-1B coaches seat 122 to 127, and the Pullman-built BTC-1C seats 114. The MBTA is phasing the fleet out in favor of bi-levels.

singleCab@mbta.about: The CTC-1B is a single-level cab car that lets a train run push-pull. Of 53 owned, about 20 are in service. The older single-level fleet is being phased out in favor of bi-level cars.

silverliner4.about: The Silverliner IV is a stainless steel EMU that became SEPTA's standard Regional Rail car. 232 were built. After fires in 2025, the FRA ordered inspections of the whole fleet, and SEPTA is working toward replacing it.

silverliner5@septa.about: The Silverliner V is a stainless steel EMU built in South Korea with final assembly in South Philadelphia. It replaced Silverliner II and III cars from the 1960s. SEPTA pulled all 120 from service in 2016 over fatigue cracks in the trucks.

acs64@septa.about: SEPTA's 15 ACS-64s, numbered 901–915, entered service in July 2018. They replaced the last AEM-7 locomotives and an ALP-44 on push-pull express trains. The design is derived from Siemens' EuroSprinter and Vectron locomotives.

pushPullCab.about: These cab cars, numbered 2401–2410, let a locomotive-hauled Regional Rail train be driven from the rear. SEPTA uses them with push-pull coaches behind ACS-64 locomotives. SEPTA has also acquired 24 used Exo (Montreal) coaches and cab cars.

pushPullCoach.about: SEPTA's push-pull trailers are 25 cars from 1987 (2501–2525) and 10 from 1999 (2550–2559). The 1987 cars seat 131 and the 1999 cars seat 117 and have a center door for high-platform boarding only. They run in locomotive-hauled trains.

mp36@metra.about: Metra was the only railroad to order the MP36PH-3S, buying 27 units numbered 401–427. Starting in 2015 Metra replaced the static inverter with a separate head-end power generator, converting all of them to MP36PH-3C specification by 2020.

sd70mach.about: Progress Rail rebuilds former Kansas City Southern de México SD70MACs for Metra with head-end power and Tier 3 emissions. They are numbered 500–541 and are Metra's first six-axle passenger locomotives since the F40C. The first entered revenue service in late 2023, and final deliveries are expected by the end of 2027.

gallery.about: Gallery cars have seats on a lower level and on narrow balconies along the sides of the upper level. Metra's come from Budd (1950s–70s), Amerail (1990s) and Nippon Sharyo (2002–05) and seat roughly 150 to 160. Metra has ordered Alstom Coradia bi-levels to replace the older cars, with first delivery expected in 2027.

galleryCab.about: Gallery cab cars let Metra trains run push-pull. Many Metra cab cars are coach/cab units that also carry passengers, built by Budd, Morrison-Knudsen/Amerail and Nippon Sharyo. Metra has ordered Alstom Coradia bi-levels to replace the older cars.

highliner.fleet: 160 with Metra (26 more leased to South Shore Line)
highliner.about: Highliner II cars run on the electrified Metra Electric District and replaced 1970s Highliners. Each car has four 200 hp motors and a stainless steel body. Metra owns 26 more that are leased to the South Shore Line.

silverliner5@rtd.about: RTD calls these cars EMU V. They run on its A, B, G and N lines and use 25 kV 60 Hz overhead power only. They share a base design with SEPTA's Silverliner V, but RTD's has less powerful traction motors and full-width cabs.

mp36@frontrunner.about: UTA's FrontRunner commuter rail between Ogden and Provo uses MP36PH-3Cs. UTA bought 21 in total, then sold two to the MBTA (units 13 and 14) and one to Northstar in Minnesota. Trains on the line run at up to 79 mph.

bilevel@frontrunner.about: FrontRunner's 200-series bi-level coaches have been delivered since 2007 in several batches. UTA bought five more used bi-levels from San Diego's Coaster in December 2024. The cars are 85 feet long.

bilevelCab@frontrunner.about: FrontRunner's 100-series cab cars, numbered 101–122, let trains reverse direction without turning the locomotive. UTA bought the first in 2006 and added ten more in 2010.

gtwCar.about: CapMetro Rail runs ten GTW 2/6 diesel railcars on its 32-mile Red Line between Leander and Downtown Austin. Each is an articulated three-section vehicle: two passenger modules joined to a central diesel power module. Six were bought in 2005 and four more arrived in 2017.

gtwPower.about: The center section of each GTW holds the diesel engines and generators; the two lightweight passenger sections on either side each ride on one bogie and rest on the power module. The power module drives the train through electric traction. CapMetro's units use two 375 kW traction generators, for about 1,010 hp total.

bl36.about: Tri-Rail is the BL36PH's only customer, with 12 units numbered 818–829 (ten ordered in 2011, two added later). A separate 670 hp Caterpillar generator supplies head-end power. They replaced older F40PHL-2 locomotives built in 1968.

bilevel@trirail.about: Tri-Rail introduced the Bombardier BiLevel design to the U.S. in 1989. Its 15 coaches are numbered 1001–1015, and most have been converted to bicycle cars with 128 seats.

bilevelCab@trirail.about: These ten cab cars, numbered 512–521, were bought with 14 coaches in a deal approved in 2010 for about $95 million. They have front and rear crumple zones. Tri-Rail also owns older Bombardier cab cars.

kiss.about: Caltrain's KISS trainsets replaced its diesel trains when electric service began on August 11, 2024. Each seven-car set is about 599 feet long, with an average of about 85–100 seats per car. They can reach 110 mph but Caltrain operates at up to 79 mph.

kissCab.type: Bi-level electric multiple unit cab car
kissCab.about: Each Caltrain KISS trainset has a cab car at either end, numbered 301–346; the truck away from the cab is powered. Trainsets have been in service since August 2024. They can reach 110 mph, but Caltrain runs them at up to 79 mph.

smartDmu.about: SMART's self-propelled diesel cars run between Sonoma and Marin counties in California. Each car has a Cummins QSK19 engine and bike racks, and regular service runs trains in pairs or triplets. The first set arrived in April 2015.

f125.about: Metrolink is the F125's only customer, with 40 units numbered 903–942, and has run them since 2016. Delivery was years behind schedule. In March 2026, Metrolink cut its schedule by 20%, citing poor reliability and high maintenance cost.

bilevel@metrolink.about: Metrolink's Bombardier coaches were delivered in three batches (1992–93, 1997 and 2002), part of what Metrolink calls its Sentinel fleet. Most of the 1997 batch is not in service.

bilevelCab@metrolink.about: Metrolink calls these crash-energy-management cars the Guardian fleet. They have an elevated engineer's compartment and absorb energy in a collision. They were built in South Korea, with final assembly in Colton, California.

flirtCar.about: Metrolink's Arrow service between San Bernardino and Redlands opened in 2022 with three FLIRT diesel multiple units. A hydrogen fuel-cell version, the first in the U.S., entered service on September 13, 2025.

flirtPower.about: The power module sits between the passenger sections and supplies electricity to the traction motors, so the train needs no overhead wire. On Arrow's diesel units it holds a diesel engine and generator. On the hydrogen unit it holds fuel cells.

mp54ac.about: GO's newest locomotive type, powered by two Cummins QSK60 engines (2,700 hp each) to meet Tier 4 emissions rules. Prototype 647 was rebuilt from an MP40PH-3C and delivered in late 2015; GO had planned more conversions but ordered 16 new-build units (667-682) instead, which GO classes as MP40PHT-T4AC.

mp40.about: The mainstay of GO Transit's diesel fleet, with a 16-cylinder EMD 710 engine. It replaced most of the older F59PH units and can haul 12-coach trains instead of 10. Unit 647 was later rebuilt as the MP54AC prototype.

bilevel@go.fleet: About 979 BiLevel cars (coaches and cab cars)
bilevel@go.about: Designed for GO Transit in the 1970s, the BiLevel is built in Thunder Bay, Ontario, and has been the whole GO coach fleet for decades, in series from I to IX with later cars built by Alstom. Seating varies by series, roughly 136 to 162 per coach.

bilevelCab@go.about: A BiLevel coach with a driving cab, letting GO trains run push-pull without turning the locomotive at terminals. Newer cars, redesigned from 2014, add crash energy management with a streamlined nose, crumple zones and a raised cab, and omit the front door.

charger@marc.about: MARC's newest locomotives, bought with options on Amtrak's state-corridor Charger contract. They entered revenue service on April 5, 2018 and replaced MARC's aging AEM-7 electrics, pulling trains on the Penn, Camden and Brunswick lines.

mp36@marc.about: The workhorse diesel of the MARC fleet, used on the Camden and Brunswick lines and on Penn Line trains that run beyond the wire. They entered service in 2009–2011 and replaced MARC's GP40WH-2 locomotives.

multilevel@marc.about: MARC IV coaches were ordered in 2011 as part of a 54-car purchase, using options on NJ Transit's MultiLevel contract. Most have 142 seats (34 cars); five have a restroom and about 132 seats. They let MARC retire its 1960s-era gallery cars and some single-level cars.

multilevelCab@marc.about: The cab-car version of MARC's 54-car MultiLevel order, with an engineer's compartment so trains can run push-pull with the locomotive at the back. Delivered in 2014 and used across the Penn, Camden and Brunswick lines.

bilevel@marc.about: MARC III bi-level coaches, the backbone of rush-hour Penn Line trains. Some were bought from Virginia Railway Express in 2008, and Bombardier overhauled the fleet around 2018–2020.

bilevelCab@marc.about: The cab-car version of MARC's MARC III bi-level fleet, letting trains run push-pull with the cab car leading toward Washington. Some were bought from Virginia Railway Express in 2008, and the fleet was overhauled by Bombardier around 2018–2020.

p40@ctrail.about: The first model of GE's Genesis series, built for Amtrak. Connecticut got eight ex-Amtrak units in 2005 and four more by way of NJ Transit in 2015. Amtrak's Beech Grove shops overhauled all 12 (numbers 6700–6711) between 2018 and 2024, and they now pull Hartford Line trains in CTrail colors.

gp40h@ctrail.builder: EMD (rebuilt by AMF Technotransport and National Railway Equipment)
gp40h@ctrail.about: Six ex-CSX freight units (GP38s and GP40s) that AMF rebuilt in Montreal in 1996 as GP40-2H passenger locomotives, with a separate head-end power generator. They were Shore Line East's main power for about a decade. National Railway Equipment overhauled them in 2017–2019, and they were reclassified GP40-3H. Numbers 6694–6699; they now mostly run on the Hartford Line.

mafersa@ctrail.about: Stainless-steel single-level coaches built in Brazil for Virginia Railway Express. CTDOT bought 33 of them (coaches and cab cars) in 2004 for Shore Line East, then moved them to the Hartford Line in 2022. The coaches have even numbers 1730–1774. CTDOT has ordered new Alstom single-level cars to replace them.

mafersaCab@ctrail.about: Single-level stainless-steel control cars from the same Virginia Railway Express order as the Mafersa coaches. They let a push-pull train be driven from the end away from the locomotive. All 10 went to CTDOT in 2004, numbered on the odd numbers 1701–1719.

m8@ctrail.about: The standard electric car on Metro-North's New Haven Line, owned jointly by CTDOT and the MTA. Four-car M8 sets replaced diesel trains on Shore Line East in May 2022. In 2026 the state brought diesel trains back to save about $8.8 million a year in Amtrak electricity costs, and the M8s went back to the shared New Haven Line pool.
